item.title: Tim Smiley: an anecdote
item.description:
Tim Smiley, an Fellow of my Cambridge college (Clare), died about two weeks ago. He had a long and distinguished career, holding major College offices such as Senior Tutor, while garnering academic accolades, such as becoming a Fellow of the British Academy. Although his specialism was logic, chiefly philosophical logic, we seldom spoke about technical matters, which I now regret. I’m not sure he was ever aware of the sort of work I was doing. Even today, most people find computational logic pretty obscure. But I do have one little story about him.

After dinner

As a young Fellow of Clare, I dined in College fairly regularly but never stayed late, not wanting to leave my wife at home alone. As I rose to leave, one of the other older Fellows said, “Going back to the lab, are you?” After I set him right, he went on to say, “Let me tell you a story about Tim Smiley.” I had to hear him out. “Once when he left dinner early, I asked him why and he said that he was going to gather his students and they would all dance on Wittgenstein’s grave.” (Wittgenstein is buried in Cambridge.)

The moment of truth

A few days later, I bumped into Tim and asked about this. “I never did that”, he said, “But it’s not a bad idea.”

item.title: A Summer with Claude and relative arbitrage, by Dmitriy Traytel
item.description:
In our Renaissance Philanthropy-funded project Copilots for Isabelle, we develop methods and tools that allow AI agents to conveniently interface with Isabelle. One major outcome of the project so far is Kevin Kappelmann’s PIDE MCP component1, which presents AI agents with a live view of Isabelle much like we human users have it through Isabelle/jEdit. I am trying to keep Claude entertained through ((semi-)auto-)formalization case studies using this tool; this was also the goal for my summer vacation (with a week of FLoC in the middle) where I was looking for a larger project on which Claude could work rather independently for a longer period of time. And one I would be reasonably detached from, so that I would not have the urge to check on the agent every hour.

My second cousin Misha Shkolnikov recently gave a talk at the Mathematics for the Real World 2026 conference. On his way to Odense, he stopped in Copenhagen so that I could give him a small tour of the city. Knowing before the summer that Misha was coming to visit, I decided to prepare a surprise: I asked Claude to autoformalize, in Isabelle using PIDE MCP, the main result of his joint article with Jou-Hua Lai and H. Mete Soner (not-yet-published, but in the final stages of the publication process) on the relative arbitrage problem under eigenvalue lower bounds.

Mandatory note here: I am quite clueless about financial mathematics and probability theory in general, let alone stochastic portfolio theory and relative arbitrage: e.g., I learned from the article’s first sentence that

Fernholz has introduced the concept of portfolio domination, now more commonly referred to as relative arbitrage, to rigorously capture the notion of “beating the market”.

I picked this particular result for the aforementioned detachment reasons, but also because it scored highly along the “recent work”—”short proof” curve among Misha’s recent papers available on arXiv.

Three weeks and over 100 000 lines later I had a finished Isabelle/HOL proof.

The Process

Claude was working nearly non-stop during these three weeks. I used a Claude Max 5x subscription over the summer, which has since been replaced by the Claude Team plan for scientists. The workflow was: Claude Fable 5 drafted as much as it could within its harsh token limits. When those were exhausted, Claude Opus 5 (I may have started with Opus 4.8) took over based on the current proof state, notes, and plans that Fable developed. Generally, my prompt was more or less “Formalize https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17702 in Isabelle using PIDE MCP” followed by numerous encouragements to keep going and occasional suggestions to look at the Archive of Formal Proofs before formalizing a new concept. I am in no position to discuss the mathematical aspects of this autoformalization, but I have something to say about the outcome and the challenges along the way (which will include some mathematics in case you are here solely for that purpose).

The Result

The main result, Theorem 1.1, itself has a rather complex statement. Here it is, with HTML generated from Isabelle (while hiding comments). Feel free to skip it; there is not enough context given here anyway to understand it fully. I include it here for completeness and to give a flavor of how things look.

theorem theorem_1_1:
  fixes K :: "(real^'n::finite) set"
  assumes kn: "k < CARD('n)" and L1: "1 ≤ L" and k1: "1 ≤ k"
    and cK: "compact K"
  defines "v ≡ (λz. enn2real (xval k L K z))"
  shows "(∃B :: real. ∀y. xval k L K y ≤ ennreal B)
       ∧ (∀c z. v z < c ⟶ (∃e>0. ∀y. dist z y < e ⟶ v y < c))
       ∧ visc_subsol_env2 k L K
           (interior K ∪ {x ∈ K - interior K. 0 < v x}) v
       ∧ visc_supersol_env2 k L K
           (interior K ∪ {x ∈ K - interior K. lsc_envK K v x < 0})
           (lsc_envK K v)
       ∧ (expandable K ⟶
          (∀u :: real^'n ⇒ real. ∀Bd.
            (∀c z. z ∈ K ⟶ u z < c ⟶
               (∃e>0. ∀y∈K. dist z y < e ⟶ u y < c))
            ⟶ (∀y∈K. ¦u y¦ ≤ Bd)
            ⟶ visc_subsol_env2 k L K
                 (interior K ∪ {x ∈ K - interior K. 0 < u x}) u
            ⟶ visc_supersol_env2 k L K
                 (interior K ∪ {x ∈ K - interior K. lsc_envK K u x < 0})
                 (lsc_envK K u)
            ⟶ (∀x∈K. u x = v x)))"

The formalization pulls in material from HOL-Analysis and HOL-Probability, but also six AFP entries: Disintegration, Kolmogorov_Chentsov, Levy_Prokhorov_Metric, Lower_Semicontinuous, Martingales, Standard_Borel_Spaces. I tasked Claude to explain the definitions that were introduced on top of these dependencies and to compare the statement to the one from the paper in a visual/interactive way. The output is available here and I find it surprisingly readable in that it contextualizes things better than Isabelle’s unprocessed HTML output. I am particularly fond of the nested tooltips to explore definitions (something I suggested to Claude)—we need deterministic tools that generate such a presentation of formal material. Fortunately, Isabelle/PIDE has all the markup we need already, so this is really a question of presentation.

The main question with any autoformalization is whether the theorem states the right result: I believe that it does after eyeballing the paper and the formal definitions. And after showing a more static PDF variant of the above document to Misha, the belief has only grown stronger. Needless to say, Isabelle checked the proofs, so fortunately I did not need to study those carefully.

Claude’s original formulation was spread over five lemmas with different assumptions. Two interesting things happened:

  • The first version of boundedness said something like (∃B :: real. ∀y. enn2real (xval k L K y) ≤ B), which does not achieve the intention to state that xval never returns ∞ because the conversion enn2real from extended non-negative reals to reals assigns 0::real to ∞::ennreal in Isabelle (a standard “totalization” completion as we know it from division). But in fact, Claude had proved along the way that xval k L K y is never ∞. It just managed to forget this when stating the final lemma. After realizing the issue, it was thus immediate to obtain the current formulation with the embedding of reals into extended non-negative reals on the right of the inequality.
  • The supersolution statement carried the assumption L > 1. During self-review Claude flagged this deviation from the paper’s L ≥ 1. I inquired about both where this comes from and whether L = 1 is an interesting case. The paper itself answers the latter: the special case L = 1 is sufficiently interesting to have a name in the paper: Ambrosio–Soner co-dimension mean curvature flow. On the other hand: this case has been studied before (by Ambrosio and Soner—the same Soner), to the extent that, according to Misha, in the setting of this paper he mainly considered L to be a large number. As for the former, Claude pointed to a place in the paper where the existence of an element in the open interval (1, L) is stated, thus introducing the L > 1 assumption implicitly in the middle of the proof. I also asked whether it is possible to work around this issue, and Claude managed to: I have no understanding of the corrected proof, but it yields L ≥ 1 as stated and Claude’s abridged explanation seemed to make sense to Misha (although he said it will take a week to incorporate it into the paper). For Misha, this was the most interesting outcome of the formalization.

The Formalization’s Size and Structure

The first complete proof had over 100 000 lines, which sounds impressive by human standards. From the start, I doubted that it had to be that long. Restructuring eventually shrank it by about a third (see below), although I never pushed very hard for really concise proofs. I did instruct the agents to iteratively remove lemmas that were flagged as unused when looking at the theorem dependencies (unused_thms). There were some in the end but not too many. Granted, the agents had to develop a lot of infrastructure that the authors assume to be pre-existing. And this is not counting advanced analysis and probability theory that was already in Isabelle and the AFP. On several occasions the authors’ proofs are of the form: “repeat the Larsson–Ruf argument word-by-word”, which required the agents to read more than the 17-page paper—so the de Bruijn factor may be smaller than it sounds.

The proofs the agents write consist of rather small steps. Here are for example the five most frequently used proof methods along with the number of occurrences in the current formalization:

6736 rule
6469 simp
1621 intro
1318 blast
 917 auto

Of course, different authors have different proof styles. My typical proofs consist of more autos and fewer rules, here e.g., in VeriMon (68 000 lines of Isabelle):

6962 auto
2502 simp
1259 cases
 909 blast
 890 rule

Apart from the need to deal with huge amounts of formal material, having small-step proofs is not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, proof processing is very efficient: isabelle build including document preparation finishes in under five minutes on my machine.

The first completed proof consisted of 64 theories dumped in a single session. I instructed the agents to separate generally reusable material from things that are specific to the proof and to use these abstractions and generalization to shrink the material. This exercise was repeated multiple times as new models would be released (e.g., Claude Opus 5.5). After these improvements, the formalization currently consists of only 85 000 lines structured in 12 sessions, of which 9 could become “library-style” AFP entries (roughly 70 000 lines together), two formalize the main result (13 000 lines), and one presents the result in the paper’s notation (1 800 lines). I write “could” because it is not clear to me whether this material belongs to the AFP in the current form, and I fear that I might not have enough understanding of the material to bring it into the desired form. I welcome any contribution from experts on such material (I’m thinking, e.g., of the authors of the entries the formalization uses), although I don’t want to force a formalization that may contain AI slop on anyone. I’m also trying to be conservative when it comes to AFP submissions because, as an AFP editor, I already see how much AI-generated material we are receiving—not all bad, but also by far not all good.

Misha tells me that second-order viscosity analysis, in particular the Crandall–Ishii(–Lions) result, is a standard and widely used tool in stochastic optimal control. This makes me hopeful that the present autoformalization can be useful for future formalizations in this area.

The Agents’ Laziness

Perhaps the most human trait of LLM agents is their laziness. When making TODO lists, the agents will structure them in such a way that low-hanging fruit is handled first, creating an illusion of fast progress. An example is Crandall–Ishii, which the agents had enormous respect for and thus kept postponing. Eventually, there was no way around it, but amusingly the agents went for the bare minimum and formalized only the core argument needed for Theorem 1.1, not the full Crandall–Ishii theorem. After Misha told me about Crandall–Ishii’s importance, I instructed the agents explicitly to fill this gap.

In other places, the laziness actually paid off. The agents managed to avoid formalizing stochastic integrals and Itô’s formula, both used in the paper. I cannot really say what they did instead (and whether it was better, worse, or mathematically interesting). Claude has mixed feelings about this and justifies it with the claim that developing this “Itô-calculus” machinery, which Isabelle lacks, would be a substantial project.

On PIDE MCP

Technologically, PIDE MCP was the perfect interface for the autoformalization part of the job. The MCP server gave the agents up-to-date access to Isabelle’s feedback on their edits. People using agents with isabelle build frequently want to single out non-terminating commands by introducing timeouts. Every now and then agents would produce non-terminating proofs (often when using blast), but PIDE MCP makes it easy for them to detect these issues by labeling the offending commands as “potentially non-terminating” (whereas PIDE’s standard terminology is “running”, which has a positive connotation that may confuse agents: when something is running it is often a good thing). The later refactoring bits proved more challenging: dynamic handling of sessions was not yet supported by PIDE MCP at the time (it is now), so every structure change required a restart of the MCP server (and thus a restart of Claude Code).

Miscellaneous Thoughts

This formalization was an odd experience. I consider myself an experienced formalizer and for me, completing a formalization is always accompanied by a sense of accomplishment, ownership, and understanding: now I really know how it works! These aspects were to a large degree absent here. Sure, in some sense it is satisfying to see the agents tick off boxes from their own TODO lists. But it is not the same as doing it oneself. Also, at times boxes get replaced by more boxes—a real Hydra fight typical of a large proof development—but without the understanding these boxes mean relatively little and one does not get a good grip on whether we are converging towards the goal or the agents just engage us in burning more tokens. (The agents have mixed success when estimating difficulty and their own capabilities.) In terms of learning how things work: I certainly learned some things while watching the agents work on the formalization: likely enough to understand the theorem statement, but not enough to distinguish which parts of the proof are reusable and which ones are specific to the theorem.

Odd things also happen in the brains of these machines. I get particularly annoyed when the thinking trace is shown and I see “thoughts” like “Writing Lean proof.” or complaints like “nlinarith is not available in this version of Isabelle”. At no point did I catch the agents actually mistaking Lean’s syntax for Isabelle’s—these artifacts did not make it out of the “thoughts”—but they constitute a reminder that these machines may not be as intelligent as their proof assembly capabilities suggest. A point Larry will appreciate: even during thinking, none of the agents ever complained about Isabelle’s lack of dependent types.

Where does one go from here? It seems feasible to obtain formalizations of recent mathematical results with bounded resources.2 Looking at the cost question in more detail, the subscription cost of $100 monthly must be contrasted with the (much higher) calculated API cost: Claude estimates $7 500, with roughly 9.7 billion input tokens and 20 million output tokens distributed over 30% Fable and 70% Opus (the same distribution is observed when attributing Isabelle lines to models that produced them)—here we are not counting the cleanup and restructuring that followed the first proved version of Theorem 1.1.

Which results should we focus on for this price? Many formalizers will care about the structure of the proof. The particular exercise seems to have been useful to Misha to straighten out the L = 1 case, regardless of the formalized proof structure. From the proof assistant perspective it is also interesting to compare technologies and libraries. Would it be cheaper, for instance, to autoformalize the same result in Lean? Also better tool support, especially for refactoring and making sense of definitions and statements, is dearly needed.

I included some critical thoughts above, but want to end on a positive note: the paradigm shift that these funny machines bring to proof assistants makes the work of our community more relevant than ever: formal proofs will be everywhere and easy to generate, also by non-experts. We just need good tools for inspecting and assessing the quality of the results and an army of domain experts to sieve through the mud and find the gold nuggets.

Acknowledgements. Thanks to Mohammad Abdulaziz, David Basin, Kevin Kappelmann, and Misha Shkolnikov for comments on earlier drafts of this article.

  1. Another useful MCP for Isabelle is I/Q. Have a look at the PIDE MCP preprint for an architectural comparison of PIDE MCP, I/Q, and other viable approaches connecting agents to Isabelle. ↩

  2. Since this summer, big tech companies have showcased that with unreasonable amounts of resources and in part using internal, unpublished models one can jump even higher and run even faster. Here, I report on using the technology they make available to ordinary subscribers. ↩

item.title: Plagiarism in the age of AI
item.description:
My first ever “blog post” (though not in this blog) was about how to write a research paper. I wrote it after reviewing a batch of badly-written papers for a conference, probably ITP or CADE. Later — a couple of years ago — came the campaign to oust Claudine Gay as President of Harvard on the grounds that she had committed plagiarism. Allegations of plagiarism were flying about on social media. Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, one of Gay’s main opponents, discovered that alleging plagiarism was a game that anyone could play. All of this happened shortly before the annual lecture I give at Cambridge based on that “how to write a paper” post. And it dawned on me that many of my complaints about the papers I was reviewing were really about plagiarism. It’s a tricky concept to pin down, which makes it especially convenient as a tool to ease out people who happen to be the wrong sex or colour. And now, with AI, it is automated.

Plagiarism 101

Plagiarism is generally defined as using another person’s work without acknowledgement, passing it off as your own, for example when a student copies another student’s work. In my Cambridge department, we have long followed the practice of asking students to bring their programming assignment for a brief interview where they answer a few questions about their code. If they didn’t write it, they won’t know anything about it. Getting answers from Stack Exchange also counts as plagiarism. Another case was when a student, asked to write a literature review of certain papers, simply copied and pasted paragraphs out of each one. Asked to explain himself at a disciplinary tribunal, he simply said, “I’ve always done this and no one ever cared before.” We care because he didn’t do his assignment, and he didn’t learn anything from the papers either. But how does this relate to the badly written papers I was grumbling about?

Recollections may vary, but it seemed to me that many of the papers I read back in 2015 (and before and since), began by mentioning three things.

  • the Pentium FDIV bug
  • the Ariane 5 crash
  • “Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!”

(I saw the last one quoted again in a technical document only a month ago.)

This is a curious list. The Pentium bug and the Ariane 5 crash were both high profile disasters, but they had happened in the mid-‘90s, about 20 years earlier. (Was there really nothing since?) Although they triggered a surge in formal verification, their true relevance is unclear. The first was reported by Intel to be a fabrication error — missing entries in a lookup table for floating-point division — although a recent analysis now disputes this. The second was caused by the use of old code from Ariane 4. The third, that famous (1972) quote by Edsger Dijkstra, is obvious to anyone who ever tried to get a computer to do anything reliably since about 1950. It’s not insightful, original or even pithy. It is not “These are the times that try men’s souls”. It is not even “Pigs are much bigger than you expect”.

It can’t be a coincidence that people keep making the same bad choices, now decades old. But is it plagiarism to copy another guy’s examples? You can’t copy him verbatim, nor are you allowed to paraphrase his text without attribution: both are straightforward plagiarism. But there are grey areas. What if you copy the other guy’s references, as well as the specific claims he made about them, but weave them into your own beautiful and original paragraph? If you have never looked up those sources, if you don’t know whether they back those claims, if you don’t even know whether those references exist, then (to paraphrase Jesus) you have committed plagiarism in your heart. That’s because you have no idea whether anything you have written is actually true. (This also happens when your text has been written by AI.1) But you will probably get away with it.

And ironically, for a paper submitted to a conference on formal verification, all three points are redundant. You are preaching to the converted. That motivational paragraph can be omitted altogether.

Quotations

One way to solve the problem of copying the other guy’s material is to quote him verbatim, with attribution. It’s best to quote material that does not itself cite other works, since his sources do not belong in your bibliography. And of course it needs to be pithy and quotable. The attribution has to be in full, including the page number, and you had better check it.

In the case of Dijkstra, his famous quote has often been misattributed or mangled. He is frequently called Edgar Dijkstra. His quote is rendered in many variant forms, such as “Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of bugs.”

Dijkstra even misquoted himself in his Turing Award lecture, “The Humble Programmer”, but as he omitted the quotation marks, it was okay. He was saying the same thing differently. But if you get a quote wrong, you are fabricating a quote, which is actually worse than plagiarism.

How many of those who have quoted Dijkstra have checked the original source or even know where his remark appeared? Here is the full citation, and none of it is optional.

E. W. Dijkstra. Notes on structured programming. In O.-J. Dahl, E. W. Dijkstra, and C. A. R. Hoare, editors, Structured Programming. Academic Press, 1972 (page 6).

I have owned this book and read Dijkstra’s essay, where he proves, for example, that

A factor of a thousand is already far beyond our powers of imagination!

And he offers as evidence

One can close one’s eyes and imagine how it feels to be standing in an open place, a prairie or a sea shore, while far away a big, reinless horse is approaching at a gallop, one can “see” it approaching and passing. To do the same with a phalanx of a thousand of these big beasts is mentally impossible: your heart would miss a number of beats by pure panic, if you could!

Google indicates that I am the first person in the world to quote these passages. (For completeness, they are found on page 2.) If you can’t be bothered to provide the source for your quotation, you should not be quoting it at all.

Self-plagiarism

Plagiarism is theft. So what does it mean to steal from yourself? It’s when you reuse your material inappropriately. Another of my hates from that 2015 round of refereeing was people who used the same text in their abstract, their introduction, and maybe even their conclusions. For one thing, the different parts of a paper have different purposes. You don’t use a toilet plunger as a cookie cutter. And once people notice you’re in the habit of reusing your own material, they are likely to give up altogether. I can remember a guy who gave me a bunch of his papers. I read one, then I picked up another, and another, and there were so many verbatim overlaps — whole paragraphs and worked examples — that I threw them all away.

Self-plagiarism takes another form, which I have been guilty of many times. It’s when you publish something in a conference, then submit it to a journal. The point is that a journal version will give you more views and more prestige, but you have to make it significantly longer and better than the conference version. These days you are expected to include a footnote to say that the journal version is based on your earlier work, which you should cite.

Boilerplate

A typical paper starts with an introduction to motivate the work, followed by a section on background material. This should include the concepts and notation needed to understand the rest of the paper. Formal definitions, whether mathematical or otherwise, may be copied verbatim because they involve no originality. There really is only one way to define a prime number. On the other hand, explanations and examples still count as original.

In that bleak time in 2015, I faced again an old enemy: two incomprehensible pages of definitions involving low‑level syntax: terms and formulas, occurrences (positions) in a term, substitutions, unifiers, literals, clauses and on and on. I was never sure, but it seemed to me that they were exactly the same every time, as if a file of this crap were being shared with everyone who was worried about filling their page limit.2 Occasionally, I felt like checking how many of the definitions were actually used. The paper might still be good, but often I was tempted to grab my mouse and choose Strong Reject. Material of that sort belongs in an appendix.

Another source of boilerplate material is your acknowledgements. I remember seeing Prof. Gay accused of plagiarising her acknowledgements. And I am willing to bet a considerable sum that she did not acknowledge another person’s parents, professor or boyfriend. If you write “I am grateful to X for their unstinting love and support, to Professor Y for their wise and insightful advice, and to Z for not letting me give up”, you will score highly on the plagiarism detector. Fortunately, it doesn’t matter.

The penalty

Since people have been drummed out of their jobs for plagiarism, it’s worth thinking about how it should be punished. For Cambridge students in straightforward cases, the rule is simple: the copied work receives zero credit. So the penalty hinges on how much was copied and how important it was, which is fair. Copying a few sentences for your introduction may cost you nothing beyond the ordeal of the disciplinary tribunal. No one cares about the acknowledgements at all. If, on the other hand, you have copied the heart of the work, you are likely to get a zero. And that could easily mean failing the course.

It’s remarkable how many media commentators seem to think that plagiarism is some sort of ultimate crime, especially for those of the wrong sex or colour. But it is not a crime in any legal sense: it is a form of academic misconduct and more common than many people realise. The appropriate response depends on what was copied and why. The same pundits who rage about alleged plagiarism seem to fall silent when other academics are implicated in actual and serious crimes.

What about AI?

Today, journals are overwhelmed by papers generated using AI. Some people say they should all be desk-rejected: AI sucks at writing, sometimes fabricates references and is an automated plagiarism machine to boot. It has been trained on existing texts and has been seen to output known texts verbatim.

We need to distinguish between papers generated using AI and those written with the assistance of AI. How can you benefit from AI as an author?

I find that AI is helpful at reminding me of things I should know but can’t easily recall. It might be good at suggesting things to cover in your introduction or conclusions. Perhaps, with the right prompt, you’ll get “the point of this work” (intro) as separate and distinct from “what has been learned from this work” (conclusions). And you can limit your abstract to five sentences.

AI can help analyse, manage, transform and present your experimental data. You still need to check that it did the job right. It is good at suggesting relevant references. You still have to locate them, check their details and actually read them, at least in part. (With a well-written paper, the abstract and conclusions should give you the essence.) One of my pet hates is too-long abstracts, introductions and conclusions, so do not allow AI to fill yours with drivel.

For non‑native speakers forced to write in English, the temptation to let AI do the job must be overwhelming. And yet your own English will likely more focused and coherent than anything that AI can write for you. If pressed for time, it may work to write in your native language and then ask a model to perform a literal translation. It will at least be your own voice.

Once you’ve got a first draft, a good language model is the best ever proofreader. I’ve been notified of everything from basic typos to LaTeX errors (the kind where LaTeX silently gives you the wrong output) to duplicate ORCID numbers and inconsistent punctuation. It can even notice mathematical errors and editorial bias. Just remember that it can sometimes be wrong.

Finally, AI is great when you get a pile of reports from not very happy referees. It will digest them for you, returning a well-organised summary of things you need to fix, why and for whom. Use AI for what it’s good at, not to plagiarise other people’s prose for you.
